title: Three Maritime Chokepoints Under Siege Threaten a Quarter of Global Oil Supply
excerpt: From the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea to the Black Sea, converging conflicts are redrawing the map of global energy trade — and India is already adapting.
body:
• Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi embargo on Saudi Red Sea ports have slashed Middle East oil exports to roughly 6.2 million barrels per day — less than a third of pre-war levels.
  • Oman has presented Iran with a Gulf-backed plan for voluntary shipping fees at Hormuz, modelled on the Strait of Malacca system, but Tehran rejected it, demanding broader control.
  • India's Mangalore Refinery has issued a crude purchase tender explicitly requiring suppliers to avoid both the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, signalling a structural shift in buying patterns.
  • The simultaneous disruption of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, and the Black Sea collectively imperils roughly a quarter of global seaborne oil supply.

The global economy is facing an energy crisis without modern precedent. Three of the world's most critical maritime chokepoints — the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea, and Black Sea shipping lanes — are simultaneously under threat from converging conflicts, collectively endangering roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil supply.

Combined oil exports from the Persian Gulf and Saudi Arabia's west coast have plunged to around 6.2 million barrels per day this week, according to data analytics firm Kpler. That figure is less than half the wartime peak of 13.4 million bpd hit in late June and far below the more than 20 million bpd that typically flowed from the region before the U.S.-Iran war began in February.

Hormuz: The World's Most Valuable Chokepoint

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before the conflict, remains the primary front. Iran effectively shut the strait to non-Iranian vessels after the U.S.-Israeli strikes on February 28, and a deal signed last month to partially reopen it collapsed in early July when Iran fired on ships using a channel it had not approved.

https://x.com/Lahcenhaddad/status/2083816483419816082

Oman this week presented Tehran with a Gulf-backed proposal for a compromise: Iran would help administer the strait alongside Oman and collect voluntary fees from vessels, a system analogous to the one governing the Strait of Malacca, where Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore ask ships to pay voluntary contributions for navigation and safety services, according to Reuters.

"The strait is an international waterway, and Iran cannot control or restrict transit through it. Iran is overreaching with unreasonable demands."

— U.S. State Department official, as quoted by the Wall Street Journal

Iran rejected the Omani proposal. Tehran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran wants to manage one-way shipping through its side of the strait entirely and part of the opposite direction. Washington has repeatedly rejected any tolls or fees, calling them illegal under international maritime law.

The Red Sea: A Second Front Opens

On July 20, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels declared a complete naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, opening a dangerous second front. Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports had emerged as a critical alternative export route after Hormuz was shut down, handling four to five million barrels per day through pipeline networks connecting the kingdom's oil fields to the coast.

The Houthis have already claimed missile and drone strikes on two Saudi oil tankers — the Encelia and the Layla — near the port of Jizan. Five tankers changed course in the Red Sea to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait last week, and three tankers loaded with Saudi oil bound for China and India made U-turns, according to Reuters.

Ali Akbar Velayati, senior advisor to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, wrote on social media that Iran's "Resistance front views Bab el-Mandeb as it does Hormuz," warning that "the flow of global energy and trade can be disrupted with a single move."

The Black Sea: A Third Pressure Point

Meanwhile, Ukraine has mounted sustained attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and shipping near the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, which handles nearly a third of Russia's oil exports. Strikes have paused flows through a pipeline carrying Russian and Kazakh oil to the Black Sea, further tightening global supply.

The convergence of these three disruptions marks a scenario energy analysts had long feared but rarely expected to materialize simultaneously.

India Adapts as Markets Shift

Indian buyers are among the first to formally adjust. India's state-owned Mangalore Refinery this week issued a crude purchase tender that, for the first time, explicitly asked suppliers to avoid both the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters. The move effectively requires suppliers to use longer, more expensive routes regardless of how U.S.-Iran negotiations develop.

"The issue is not just the sheer volume of oil that typically transits the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but that the loss of a guarantee of safe passage would represent a further contraction of viable oil and liquefied natural gas trade routes."

— Clara Gillispie, energy and climate expert, Council on Foreign Relations

Broader Asian and European importers of Middle East LNG are also planning to seek lower prices and stronger supply guarantees from Qatar and the UAE, signalling that the risk premium for Gulf energy may become permanent. Higher insurance premiums, elevated shipping costs, and persistent security concerns are increasingly seen as the structural cost of doing business in the region.

What Comes Next

Diplomatic channels remain open but strained. President Trump called off U.S. airstrikes over the weekend after 13 nights of renewed bombing, saying there were "good talks" under way — but threatened to restart if negotiations stall. Iran has denied seeking new talks. Mediators from Pakistan, Qatar, Turkey, and Egypt are working to resolve ambiguities in the preliminary peace framework signed last month.

Oil prices tumbled roughly 8% on Monday after the bombing pause, with Brent crude falling below $84 a barrel. But analysts warn the volatility cuts both ways: any resumption of hostilities could send prices surging back toward the $200-per-barrel scenario that Houthi officials have openly warned about.

For the moment, the Middle East appears to be drifting toward what Reuters columnist Ron Bousso has called "a new equilibrium in which energy continues to flow but under a constant shadow of coercion." Whether that equilibrium can hold without tipping into full-scale confrontation remains the defining question of the crisis.
nri_angle: India's Mangalore Refinery has issued an unprecedented crude purchase tender requiring suppliers to avoid the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, signalling a structural shift in how Indian energy buyers navigate the crisis.
